Plot Gallery

Source: vignettes/plot-gallery.Rmd
plot-gallery.Rmd

Overview

This gallery shows every plotting function of NanoQuRe on the dataset bundled with the package, first with its default settings and then with the arguments that change the picture. Each plot is followed by a short note on how it may be read and on what it cannot show. All plots are interactive: hovering over a trace displays the underlying values, and the legend toggles individual traces.

Example data

Two datasets are used. The bundled sample_data object holds 1000 reads of a single MinION run and serves the read length and Q-score distributions. Its reads come from the first minutes and the last half hour of the run only, so it cannot illustrate the plots that follow a run over time.

library(NanoQuRe)

data(sample_data)

The time-resolved plots therefore use a simulated run, generated below: 200,000 reads on 512 channels over 48 h, in which channels stop producing reads at different times and both the translocation speed and the Q-score decline slowly. These data are artificial. They only illustrate what the plots look like for a complete run and carry no biological meaning.

set.seed(123) # reproducible simulation

n_reads <- 200000
n_channels <- 512
run_seconds <- 48 * 3600

# each channel stops producing reads at its own time
channel_end <- pmin(stats::rweibull(n_channels, shape = 1.5, scale = 30) * 3600,
                    run_seconds)
# channels that live longer contribute more reads
channel <- sample(seq_len(n_channels), n_reads, replace = TRUE, prob = channel_end)
start_time <- stats::runif(n_reads, min = 0, max = channel_end[channel])
run_fraction <- start_time / run_seconds

# log-normal read lengths; speed and quality decline over the run
read_length <- round(stats::rlnorm(n_reads, meanlog = 6.8, sdlog = .9)) + 20
speed <- stats::rnorm(n_reads, mean = 400 - 60 * run_fraction, sd = 25)
qscore <- stats::rnorm(n_reads, mean = 12.5 - 2 * run_fraction, sd = 2)

simulated_run <- data.frame(
  sample_id = "simulated_run",
  run_id = "simulated_run_1",
  channel = channel,
  start_time = start_time,
  duration = read_length / pmax(speed, 50),
  sequence_length_template = read_length,
  mean_qscore_template = qscore,
  # pass/fail threshold of the simulated basecaller
  passes_filtering = qscore >= 9
)

Every function returns an ordinary plotly object (plot_double() returns a named list of two), which can be modified with plotly functions or embedded in an R Markdown document. The summary tables and generate_report() are described in the Getting Started and Using Individual Functions vignettes.

Read length and quality

plot_read_lengths()

The plot shows a histogram of read lengths drawn as a step line, with sequence length in nt on the x axis (logarithmic by default) and the number of reads per bin on the y axis. Vertical lines mark the mean read length and the N50.

plot_read_lengths(sample_data)

With weight = "bases", each bin is scaled by the number of bases it contains instead of the number of reads, which shifts the visual weight towards long reads.

plot_read_lengths(sample_data, weight = "bases")

A linear axis combined with upper_limit truncates the view; reads beyond the limit are counted in a note at the top right of the plot.

plot_read_lengths(sample_data, log_x = FALSE, upper_limit = 5000)

Because the result is an ordinary plotly object, it can be modified further with plotly functions.

length_plot <- plot_read_lengths(sample_data)
plotly::layout(length_plot, title = list(text = "Read lengths, MinION run"))

Reading the plot. In sample_data the mean read length is 1083 nt, the median is 712 nt, and the N50 is 1201 nt; the mean and N50 lie well to the right of the bulk of the reads because a few very long reads (the longest is 43360 nt; 10 reads exceed 10000 nt) pull both upwards. The base-weighted view shows the same effect: reads longer than 10000 nt are 1% of reads but carry about 24% of the bases. The plot describes length only; it says nothing about the quality of those reads or about when in the run they were produced.

plot_quality_distribution()

The plot shows a stacked histogram of the mean Q-score of each read (x axis) against the number of reads (y axis), with fail reads and pass reads in separate colours. A dashed vertical line marks the user-defined cut-off (qscore_cutoff), and a solid line marks the lowest Q-score among pass reads, which approximates the basecaller threshold.

plot_quality_distribution(sample_data)

Raising qscore_cutoff moves the dashed line, which is useful for judging how many reads would remain under a stricter custom filter.

plot_quality_distribution(sample_data, qscore_cutoff = 10)

Reading the plot. In sample_data 885 reads pass and 115 fail; the basecaller threshold is at about Q8.01, so the default cut-off of Q7 lies below it and 61 fail reads sit above that line. The median read Q-score is 11.29, and 300 reads fall below Q10. The histogram describes per-read means only; it cannot show how quality varies within a read, nor why a given read failed.

plot_double()

The function returns a named list of two plots that share the same x axis, time since the start of the run in hours. length_plot shows the maximum, average, and minimum read length per hour on a logarithmic y axis, and qscore_plot shows the maximum, average, and minimum mean Q-score per hour. Because sample_data covers only two short periods of a run, the plots below use the simulated run described above.

double_plots <- plot_double(simulated_run)
double_plots$length_plot
double_plots$qscore_plot

Reading the plot. These data are simulated and only illustrate the plot. The average Q-score falls from 12.47 in the first hour to 11.48 in hour 23 and 10.50 in hour 47, a slow decline of the kind that may indicate pore or flow cell ageing in a real run. The average read length stays near 1350 nt throughout, whereas the maximum varies widely from hour to hour (27660 nt in the first hour, 15709 nt in the last), because it is determined by single reads and is sensitive to the number of reads in each hour. The plots show per-hour extremes and means only, so they cannot reveal how many reads contribute to each hour or which channels are responsible for a change.

Yield, throughput, and speed

plot_cumulative_yield()

The plot shows the cumulative number of sequenced bases (in Gb, y axis) against the start time of the reads (in hours, x axis), with one trace for pass reads and one for fail reads. Reads are sorted by start time and summed in order; the value at each time bin is the running total at its last read, and max_points caps the number of bins per trace (a bin is never narrower than one minute). The examples in this section use the simulated run, so the numbers illustrate the plots and carry no biological meaning.

plot_cumulative_yield(simulated_run)

Restricting the input to the first 12 h of the run, with a small max_points, gives a coarser trace over a shorter time axis.

first_12h <- simulated_run[simulated_run$start_time < 12 * 3600, ]
plot_cumulative_yield(first_12h, max_points = 50L)

The returned object is an ordinary plotly object, so it can be modified with plotly functions, for example to change the title and the x axis range.

yield_plot <- plot_cumulative_yield(simulated_run)
plotly::layout(
  yield_plot,
  title = list(text = "Cumulative yield, first 24 h"),
  xaxis = list(range = c(0, 24))
)

Reading the plot. The pass reads reach about 0.249 Gb and the fail reads about 0.024 Gb (8.8% of reads fail) by the end of the 48 h. The slope of the pass trace flattens over time, which suggests that fewer reads were started in the later hours, in line with the channels in the simulation stopping one after another. The plot cannot indicate why the slope changes, because a loss of active pores, a loss of library, and a change in read length all lower it.

plot_seq_throughput()

The plot shows the yield per hour (in Gb, y axis) against run time (in hours, x axis), separately for pass and fail reads. Each read is assigned to the hour in which it started, the read lengths of each hour are summed, and every hour between the first and the last read is included, with hours without reads set to zero.

plot_seq_throughput(simulated_run)

The same plot for the first 12 h of the run, which shows the early hours at a finer scale.

plot_seq_throughput(first_12h)

Reading the plot. The pass throughput is highest in the first hour (about 0.0103 Gb) and falls to about 0.0050 Gb in hour 23 and about 0.0009 Gb in hour 47, whereas the fail throughput stays between about 0.0003 and 0.0006 Gb per hour. A decline of this kind may reflect pores becoming inactive, but the plot does not show which channels stopped. Hours without reads appear as zero yield and cannot be told apart from an interruption of the run, and a long read is counted wholly in the hour in which it started.

plot_average_speed()

The plot shows the mean translocation speed (in nt/s, y axis) per hour of run time (x axis) for pass and fail reads. The speed of an hour is the summed read length divided by the summed read duration of the reads that started in that hour, which weights long reads more heavily than a mean of per-read speeds.

plot_average_speed(simulated_run)

The same plot for pass reads only, which removes the noisier fail trace and makes the trend of the pass reads easier to follow.

pass_reads <- simulated_run[simulated_run$passes_filtering, ]
plot_average_speed(pass_reads)

Reading the plot. The pass speed declines from about 398 nt/s in hour 0 to about 384 nt/s in hour 11, about 370 nt/s in hour 23, and about 339 nt/s in hour 47, and the fail reads follow almost the same course. A slow decline of this kind is commonly attributed to ageing of the flow cell or depletion of reagents, although the plot alone cannot confirm a cause. The speed is derived from the duration field of the sequencing summary and is not a direct measurement of motor kinetics, and hours without reads would appear as gaps in the line.

Channel activity

The plots of this group use the simulated run (simulated_run) described above; the data are artificial and only illustrate the plots.

plot_active_channels()

The plot shows the number of channels with at least one read overlapping each time window. Dashed lines mark the first window in which the count falls to the given fractions (thresholds) of the highest count in the first hour; the final window, which is usually partial, is not searched.

plot_active_channels(simulated_run)

A wider window (one hour instead of ten minutes) smooths the short-term fluctuations of the count.

plot_active_channels(simulated_run, bin_width = 1)

Other fractions of the first-hour maximum can be marked with thresholds.

plot_active_channels(simulated_run, thresholds = c(.75, .5, .25))

A threshold that is never reached is reported in a note on the plot instead of a dashed line; here 5% of the first-hour maximum is not reached.

plot_active_channels(simulated_run, thresholds = c(.5, .25, .05),
                     bin_width = 1)

Reading the plot. All 512 channels produced reads in simulated_run, and the first-hour maximum is 479 active channels with the default window (512 with bin_width = 1). With the default window, the count falls to 50% of that maximum at 24.5 h and to 25% at 36.5 h; the final window still holds 55 active channels (about 11%) and, with one-hour windows, the last window holds 63 (about 12%), which is why the 5% line is absent. A channel without reads in a window is not necessarily exhausted, and pore scans and pauses are not recorded in the sequencing summary, so a decline of the count may reflect several processes that these data cannot separate.

pore_activity_heatmap()

The figure has two panels: the upper one shows bases per channel per time bin (channels on the x axis, run time on the y axis), and the lower one shows bases per channel arranged according to the physical layout of the flow cell.

pore_activity_heatmap(simulated_run)

A coarser time bin reduces the number of rows of the upper panel.

pore_activity_heatmap(simulated_run, bin_width = 6)

The PromethION layout is illustrated with a second, small simulated summary (3000 reads on channels 1 to 3000, one run_id, 24 h) that only illustrates the 3000-channel layout.

set.seed(123) # reproducible simulation
n_prom <- 3000
prom_summary <- data.frame(
  run_id = "simulated_promethion_1",
  sample_id = "simulated_promethion",
  channel = sample(seq_len(3000), n_prom, replace = TRUE),
  start_time = stats::runif(n_prom, min = 0, max = 24 * 3600),
  duration = stats::rlnorm(n_prom, meanlog = 1, sdlog = .7),
  sequence_length_template = round(stats::rlnorm(n_prom, meanlog = 7.5,
                                                 sdlog = .8)),
  mean_qscore_template = stats::rnorm(n_prom, mean = 11, sd = 2)
)
prom_summary$passes_filtering <- prom_summary$mean_qscore_template >= 9

pore_activity_heatmap(prom_summary, platform = "promethion", bin_width = 2)

Reading the plot. In simulated_run, the 100 channels with the most bases account for about 36% of the 273 million bases and the 100 channels with the fewest for about 5%, so the yield per channel is uneven. Dark cells in the upper panel show when and on which channels the bases were produced; the lower panel shows whether high and low yields cluster in regions of the flow cell. The summary data do not identify the physical cause of differences between channels or regions. The function requires a single run_id, and channel numbers outside the selected layout (1 to 512 for MinION, 1 to 3000 for PromethION) stop it with an error, so platform has to match the data. Flongle flow cells are not supported.
